summary: AstroHealth is an educational health-monitoring prototype for crews on long space missions. It combines heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, sleep duration and daily mood in Flight Log, a four-view interface for reviewing observations, charts, explained alerts and journal entries. Using a reproducible 30-day synthetic mission, the backend compares readings with an individual experimental reference and highlights sustained resting heart-rate changes. Every observation retains its timestamp, measurement context and source; missing data and insufficient history remain explicit. NASA research informed the problem framing and indicator selection. A separate pipeline processes terrestrial PhysioNet records without presenting them as astronaut data. AstroHealth supports transparent review and crew awareness; it does not diagnose illness, use real astronaut records or provide clinically validated thresholds.
details:
THE PROBLEM

During long space missions, crews need to understand changes in their health observations, including when those changes differ from their own usual patterns. A measurement without its time, context or source can be misleading. Missing observations, insufficient history and failed requests must also remain distinguishable from reassuring results.

AstroHealth addresses the challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions” through an educational prototype that brings physiological observations and daily self-reports into one transparent monitoring workflow.

OUR SOLUTION

Flight Log, AstroHealth’s interface, provides four connected views:

• Dashboard: the latest recorded heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, sleep duration and mood, with each observation’s original timestamp and provenance.
• Analytics: mission history, individual reference comparisons, visible gaps and alternative data tables.
• Alerts: experimental attention cues with their triggering observations, reference values, evaluation windows and explanations.
• Journal: daily sleep, mood and notes, with validation, correction and save feedback.

Users can review earlier mission days without allowing later observations to appear in those historical views. The interface supports light and dark themes and clearly identifies synthetic mission data.

HOW IT WORKS

A seeded generator creates a reproducible 30-day fictional mission. Validated imports store profiles, readings, journal entries and source information in SQLite. A FastAPI backend serves this information to the React frontend through a typed HTTP client.

The experimental reference uses observations from mission days 1–5 and becomes available from day 6 when sufficient history exists. Vital-sign comparisons use resting observations rather than mixing rest, exercise and sleep contexts. Daily sleep records are handled separately. Mood uses an ordinal 1–5 self-report scale and is never averaged into a physiological baseline.

The prototype implements one demonstration rule, DEMO-HR-CHANGE: resting heart rate at least 5 beats/min above the individual reference on two consecutive mission days produces an explained warning. A later resting observation below that threshold resolves the event. This threshold is a simulation convention, not a medical recommendation or NASA standard.

DEMONSTRATED MISSION SCENARIO

The synthetic mission establishes a resting heart-rate reference of 72.2 beats/min. An isolated spike on day 9 does not trigger the sustained-change rule. Missing observations on days 12–14 remain explicit. Sustained changes on days 18–19 produce a warning on day 19; the event resolves on day 22 after a later observation falls below the demonstration threshold.

The scenario also includes a second fictional profile with insufficient history. This lets reviewers distinguish insufficient data from a completed evaluation with no active alerts.

DATA AND SCIENTIFIC GROUNDING

NASA Human Research Program publications informed the project’s problem framing and indicator selection. Resources on exploration-atmosphere hypoxia provided context for oxygen monitoring; Behavioral Health and Performance research informed the inclusion of daily self-reports.

These publications are scientific references, not NASA datasets ingested by the application, and they do not validate our demonstration threshold.

A separate pipeline processes a small subset of the PhysioNet BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset. These are terrestrial clinical records, explicitly identified as such. They are never relabeled as astronaut observations or loaded into the fictional astronaut mission.

HUMAN-CENTERED DESIGN

Flight Log emphasizes recognition, consistency and visibility of system status. Observations retain their units, context and timestamps. Loading, request failure, missing records and insufficient analysis have distinct presentations. Historical views are clearly identified.

Charts include data-table alternatives. Attention states use text and icons alongside color. Journal validation, cancellation, unsaved-change prompts and retained drafts support error prevention and recovery. These decisions draw on Nielsen’s usability heuristics and Laws of UX; they do not constitute a completed usability study or accessibility certification.

TECHNOLOGY AND VERIFICATION

The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts and Lucide. The backend uses FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn, Pandas and SQLite.

Documented automated checks cover data generation, experimental rules, API behavior, historical cutoffs, repeated imports, frontend response handling and persistence after service restart. Browser acceptance records and remaining manual checks are maintained separately in the repository.

IMPACT AND LIMITATIONS

The intended benefit is clearer crew awareness and more traceable review of changing observations. The prototype demonstrates how individual references, explicit uncertainty and understandable explanations can support that workflow.

AstroHealth is not a diagnostic system. It has no clinical validation, real astronaut health records or live wearable integration. Its mission data and profiles are fictional, its alert rule is experimental, and broader accessibility and user evaluation remain future work. Internal trend calculations are not yet exposed as dedicated API fields.

Next steps include evidence-reviewed rules, provenance-preserving sensor integration, usability studies and broader accessibility evaluation.

dataRefs: NASA HRP — Exploration Atmosphere Hypoxia: scientific background for oxygen-monitoring context; not an ingested dataset or a source of our alert threshold.
NASA Behavioral Health and Performance Standard Measures: informed the inclusion of subjective mood self-reports; our 1–5 scale is not a validated NASA instrument.
NASA HRP — Behavioral Health Evidence Report: background on behavioral-health monitoring during long missions; no diagnostic model or threshold was adopted.
NASA exploration-atmosphere exercise study: research reference for interpreting oxygen measurements in context, not astronaut data imported into AstroHealth.
NASA Brand Guidelines: reference consulted for visual identity and attribution; use does not imply endorsement.
projectRefs: PhysioNet BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset v1.0.0 — terrestrial clinical data processed separately; ODC-By v1.0; never presented as astronaut observations.
Pimentel et al. — original BIDMC respiration-estimation publication associated with the dataset.
Barger et al., 2014 — spaceflight sleep research informing the project’s sleep-monitoring motivation.
Norsk et al., 2015 — published spaceflight cardiovascular research used as scientific context.
Prisk, 2019 — pulmonary challenges of prolonged space travel; research background for respiratory monitoring.
Smith et al., 2024 — review of lung physiology in space; contextual research, not a source of validated project thresholds.
Canadian Space Agency — Bio-Monitor: reference example of physiological monitoring in space.
Canadian Space Agency — CCISS: cardiovascular research reference.
AstroHealth synthetic mission — reproducible fictional 30-day data, generation instructions and scenario documentation.
Complete research bibliography, data provenance, source categories, licenses and attribution.

Backend software dependencies — FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn and Pandas; exact versions are listed.
Backend testing dependencies and verification tools.
